1950-kirkcaldy.label: Kirkcaldy and Glenrothes
1950-kirkcaldy.text: Born on 18 June 1950 in Kirkcaldy, he grew up in Glenrothes and in Prinlaws, the paper-mill village by Leslie. His father was a travelling salesman and later a carpet fitter. His mother came from Blyth in Northumberland and brought her Geordie speech with her to Fife. In the coal shed of their council house she kept a shrine to “Black Sophia”.
1950-kirkcaldy.bildtext: Jackie Leven as a child · Illustration

1971-dorset.label: Sturminster Marshall, Dorset
1971-dorset.text: A fall from his bicycle, at night, on the way home from the pub along a Dorset lane. Leven had come south out of what he called the maelstrom of living dangerously in the North; the band, the attack and the heroin were all still ahead of him. More than thirty years later he described this moment as his first peace.

1977-doll-by-doll.label: Formosa Street, London W9
1977-doll-by-doll.text: The band came together in a squatted basement in Formosa Street, Maida Vale. Their road manager Colin delivered the calendar to the fifty most important people in the London music business by throwing the copies into their reception areas. The band went on to make four albums, get thrown off two other bands’ tours, and record a fifth album that has never been released.
1977-doll-by-doll.bildtext: Jackie Leven in the Doll by Doll years · Illustration

1978-bristol-gardens.label: The squatted quarter
1978-bristol-gardens.text: Bristol Gardens, Formosa Street, Clifton Villas: crumbling ochre houses with Moorish arched windows, home, by Leven’s own account, to Scottish gangs, prostitutes, heroin addicts, Western Sufis and several desperate rock bands. When his parents came to visit they turned out to be hard drinkers, and his mother made friends with the landlady of the George.

1983-caledonian-road.label: North London
1983-caledonian-road.text: Walking home to Maida Vale, just off the Caledonian Road, Leven was attacked and his throat was injured. For a long time afterwards he could not sing, for a while he could not speak, and the heroin years followed. The evening does not appear once in the 76 surviving texts he wrote himself, although he wrote publicly about his life for nine years. The sources disagree on whether it was 1983 or 1984.

1985-core-trust.label: Lisson Grove
1985-core-trust.text: After his own withdrawal Leven co-founded a centre for people with addictions in Lisson Grove and became its head counsellor, with no formal training, in buildings where he had once lived himself. The quotation comes from his account of a winter solstice night he sat through with Jason Wright to exorcise the place.

1992-oban.label: The Rowantree Hotel
1992-oban.text: After years without writing a line, Leven wrote three songs in a single afternoon in a hotel in Oban: “The Crazy Song”, “Gylen Gylen” and “Heartsick Land”. He did not yet trust himself to record again and played them to nobody, but he kept writing. He never says exactly when this was; 1992 is an estimate.

1994-mystery-of-love.label: Album · The Mystery of Love Is Greater Than the Mystery of Death
1994-mystery-of-love.text: With this album Leven came back, and it began his time with Cooking Vinyl, the label he stayed with to the end. Robert Bly recorded two poems for it at the Townhouse Studios in Shepherd’s Bush: “The Garden” by Antonio Machado and “Clay Jug” by Kabir.

2002-the-deep-pool.label: He starts to write
2002-the-deep-pool.text: From October 2002 Leven wrote a monthly column on his website, “The Deep Pool”, and from 2008 a blog and several other features. Seventy-six of these texts survive, around 90,000 words. They are the basis of this site and the only place where he talks about himself at length in his own voice. The quotation comes from one of his last entries.
2002-the-deep-pool.bildtext: Jackie Leven with glass, circa 2000 · Illustration

2004-woman-in-a-car.label: The death of his parents
2004-woman-in-a-car.text: His father died in 2000, his mother in the autumn of 2004. She could not drive, but she kept his car so that she could sit in it alone and remember, and that became the song “Woman In A Car”. When Leven cleared her room at the care home, he left her shoes and clothes behind and took away the postcards he had written to her on tour.
2004-woman-in-a-car.bildtext: Jackie Leven with guitar, circa 2006 · Illustration

2008-cottage-industry.label: Festivals, tours, fan club
2008-cottage-industry.text: Twelve flights a year with the same airline, a November tour in 2005 with fourteen dates from Solingen to Kiel, Norway on top of that, and his own fan club, Haunted Valley, run from a post office box in Derbyshire. Of the festivals he wrote that their “sudden community” had a regenerative power that could hardly be overstated.
2008-cottage-industry.bildtext: Jackie Leven with guitar, circa 2008 · Illustration

2011-ed.label: The death of his brother
2011-ed.text: His younger brother Ed died in the spring. Afterwards Leven was able to finish a song from a chorus he had begun years earlier in a hotel room in Münster: “Beware Soul Brother”. He wrote the line about snowdrops ten minutes after a walk along the Hamble, where the first ones were out. Whether Ed died in 2010 or 2011 is not certain; the site follows Leven’s own texts.

2011-belfast-of-the-mind.label: The last year in Hampshire
2011-belfast-of-the-mind.text: In his last years Leven lived in a village in Hampshire, got up at half past six and walked three miles to muck out two horses. His last entries are about the market hall clock, an orchard, the terriers in the tidal creek, and the jazz the old men play in the pub across the road.

2011-november.label: 14 November 2011
2011-november.text: Jackie Leven died on 14 November 2011 in Hampshire, aged 61. His last blog entry ends with the full text of his song “Working Alone”, an image of ploughing, of time passing and of someone else taking over the reins. For what would have been his 70th birthday, a fan had a memorial bench put up in Soho Square; it carries the last line of “Main Travelled Roads”.
